docs.title: SØAD developer guide
docs.text:
Build a complete web application using Jython controllers, SQL-backed models, and HTML views. This guide takes you from your first transaction to a protected project/task tracker deployed in a container.

You need basic programming, HTML, and SQL knowledge. You do not need to write the Java engine or use AI to follow the tutorial. SØAD, SOAD, and soad refer to the same framework; S0ADM is its development and administration interface.

docs.title: Choose your path
docs.text:
Goal Start here Learn the framework 1. Architecture, then 2. Getting started Build the complete example 3. Planning through 9. Integrations Configure or replace login 8. Authentication Work in the browser IDE 11. S0ADM and AI Use a local editor or agent 12. CLI and agents Test and deploy 13. Testing, 14. Docker, 15. Kubernetes Put this guide online 16. Publishing

Chapters have a learning sequence; the Reference navigation contains detailed contracts you can consult without interrupting the tutorial. Markdown links work in a Git browser and in the generated website.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
The tracker example includes projects, tasks, assignment to application users, status filtering, pagination, validation, private attachments, and a JSON endpoint. Members manage their own projects; an administrator permission controls destructive project deletion. Business ownership is checked independently of route permissions.

The tutorial uses the default application and MySQL, Java 21, and local application authentication. H2 is used for isolated checks. Production deployment contains the application and authentication runtime, without the S0ADM IDE.

docs.title: Version and verification
docs.text:
This guide was consolidated against the repository implementation on 2026-09-06. Consult the checked-out Gradle dependencies and soad version when comparing another installation. CLI examples were checked against executable help from commit 5342396 (a development build); installed releases may differ. The example README records reproducible verification commands and limitations.

No live account, API key, license, database password, or private registry is required merely to read or build this documentation site.

docs.title: 1. Introduction and architecture
docs.text: SØAD maps HTTP requests to small Jython classes called transactions. A transaction loads or changes database models and chooses a response: an HTML view, JSON, a download, or a redirect. Here, “transaction” names the controller; the database transaction around a request is a separate concept.

docs.title: The components
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Java engine Embedded Jetty server, configuration, JDBC pools, model generation, request context Jython runtime Transaction dispatch, rendering, authentication, filters, file uploads Application Your transactions, templates, public assets, schema, and security manifest S0ADM Browser development tools, application configuration, AI, and release preparation SOAD CLI Synchronize transaction source/views between a local workspace and S0ADM 
flowchart LR
    Developer --> IDE[S0ADM development server]
    Developer --> CLI[Local editor and SOAD CLI]
    CLI --> IDE
    IDE --> Release[Application release]
    Release --> Runtime[Application runtime]
    Browser --> Runtime
    Runtime --> DB[(Application database)]

The deployed runtime uses its own database accounts and application identities. It does not need the IDE database or an IDE session.

docs.title: Request lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant F as Transaction filters
    participant T as Transaction engine
    participant A as Application auth
    participant C as Controller
    participant D as Database
    B->>F: HTTP request
    F->>T: Continue
    T->>D: Open request database transaction
    T->>A: Authorize action
    A-->>T: Identity and access decision
    T->>C: Invoke allowed action
    C->>D: Query or update models
    C-->>T: Renderer or redirect
    T->>D: Commit on success, rollback on exception
    T-->>B: Response

Authorization failure prevents the controller action from running. Rendering is also part of request processing. External email/API calls and filesystem writes are not undone by a database rollback.

docs.title: Application layout
docs.text:
webapp/
  assets/tracker/                  public CSS and other static assets
  WEB-INF/
    jython/default/
      __init__.py
      tracker/
        __init__.py
        project.py                class Project
        _project/
          project.html
    security/app-security.json
    deploy/auth-mysql.sql
    deploy/auth-h2.sql
    classes/models/               generated; do not author or commit

/t/tracker/project invokes Project.view(ctx). /t/tracker/project/save invokes Project.save(ctx). The CLI uses an additional per-transaction directory locally; see the mapping.

docs.title: Language and database boundaries
docs.text:
Transactions run on Jython 2.7, not Python 3. Use "%s" % value instead of f-strings. Java imports work directly; CPython binary packages and pip install are not an application dependency mechanism. Put reviewed Java dependencies in the application's runtime library directory and restart.

ActiveJDBC models are generated from the live schema. Define tables first, then introspect or restart before importing new models. Business datasource support and built-in authentication support differ: the shipped local-auth SQL generator supports MySQL and H2, not every JDBC database.

Next: start a development instance.

docs.title: 2. Getting started
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you will have a development server and a working HTML transaction. Use a disposable local instance for the tutorial.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A checkout of this repository and a Java 21 JDK; set JAVA_HOME to its installation.
  • Docker or another container command compatible with the repository's development script.
  • Access to Gradle dependencies for the initial build.
  • A browser. Python 3 is needed only to build the documentation, not to run transactions.

From the repository root:

java -version
./dev.sh build
NERDCTL=docker ./dev.sh startdb
./dev.sh start
./dev.sh status

Use NERDCTL=nerdctl.lima instead if that is your installed container tool. Open http://localhost:8080/s0adm/. Use the development account configured in dev.sh; obtain its values locally rather than copying development credentials into a deployment. The script currently supplies its own IDE account defaults. Environment variables supplied before dev.sh start do not override every value it sets internally.

This workflow runs the IDE database in H2 and the application database in MySQL. Use ./dev.sh logs for startup errors and ./dev.sh stop to stop the process. NERDCTL=docker ./dev.sh stopdb stops the local database container.

If port 8080 is busy, use ./dev.sh start 9090. Check dev.sh for current DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USER, and DB_PW defaults before connecting with a database client. Do not assume the root Compose file is a clean deployment template; use the sanitized examples in this guide.

docs.title: Configure the default application
docs.text:
Open System Settings → Applications → the default application. Configure security before expecting application routes to work. For the tracker choose:

Field Value Security profile authenticated Authentication mode Application-local identity Roles admin (first), member Registration invite_only

Save, follow the one-time setup link, and set an application password. The IDE password is not copied. Keep this account flow separate from the S0ADM login. See authentication for screenshots-free field instructions and the permission grants needed by the full tracker.

docs.title: Create your first transaction
docs.text:
In the transaction editor create group web, code hello. Replace the controller:

from utils import render

class Hello(object):
    ACCESS_POLICY = {"view": "authenticated"}

    def view(self, ctx):
        ctx.output["greeting"] = "Hello from SØAD"
        ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "hello")

Save the view as _hello/hello.html within that transaction:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Hello</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>{{greeting}}</h1>
  <p>Signed in as {{current_user.full_name}}</p>
  <a href="{{logout_url}}">Sign out</a>
</body>
</html>

Save/compile and open http://localhost:8080/t/web/hello. Sign in with the application account if redirected. You should see “Hello from SØAD” and your name. For a public brochure app, choose public profile/mode and an explicit public policy instead; do not change this protected tutorial to public to bypass setup.

docs.title: Common first-run failures
docs.text:
Symptom Check No Java or build failure JAVA_HOME, Java version, Gradle dependency access Connection refused Process status, port, logs Missing models/table Correct application database; run Introspect after DDL 503 on application route Missing manifest, missing auth SQL, or mismatched checksum Redirect repeatedly to login Application account, cookie settings, HTTP vs HTTPS 404 after creating controller Group/code, capitalized class name, imports and logs

For plain HTTP development, set session_cookie_secure=false and session_cookie_samesite=LAX for the server process if its active profile requires secure cookies. Restore secure cookies for HTTPS deployment.

Next: plan the tracker.

docs.title: 3. Plan a complete application
docs.text: The tutorial is a project/task tracker for a small team. Begin with the access rules and database model, then build one working slice at a time.

docs.title: User stories and access
docs.text:
Members create projects and manage tasks inside projects they own. Each task has a title, a status, and an optional assignee selected from active application users. Assignment is informational: it does not grant access to the project. This keeps the first application's sharing model explicit and small.

Administrators can delete their own projects, including their tasks and attachments. The projects.delete permission enables the route but does not bypass ownership. Runtime user administration is a separate auth.users.manage permission granted by system_admin.

Permission admin member projects.read yes yes projects.write yes yes projects.delete yes no tasks.read yes yes tasks.write yes yes

The source examples use exactly these codes. Configure them before opening the completed application. Avoid a “catch all” public policy.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
erDiagram
    SOAD_AUTH_USER ||--o{ PROJECT : owns
    SOAD_AUTH_USER o|--o{ TASK : assigned
    PROJECT ||--o{ TASK : contains
    TASK ||--o| ATTACHMENT : holds
    PROJECT {
        int id PK
        string owner_id FK
        string name
    }
    TASK {
        int id PK
        int project_id FK
        string title
        string status
        string assignee_id FK
    }
    ATTACHMENT {
        int id PK
        int task_id FK
        blob content
        string filename
    }

Auth tables are generated by the framework. Business tables reference the local user ID but do not store passwords. Attachments are database blobs in this example so deletion and replacement participate in the same database transaction.

docs.title: Delivery milestones
docs.text:
1. Configure local auth and confirm sign-in works.
  2. Install the schema, introspect, and create projects.
  3. Add editing, filtering, pagination, and permission checks.
  4. Add tasks, status changes, assignment, and attachments.
  5. Verify cross-user access denial and JSON output.
  6. Package the release, install production auth metadata, and deploy.

For each milestone keep SQL and source together in version control. Record schema changes as ordered migrations; the CLI does not run them.

The complete implementation is under examples/tracker. Build it manually with the next chapters or use the full source as a reference. AI is an optional development path described in chapter 11.

docs.title: 4. Database and models
docs.text: SØAD generates models from the connected database. Start with SQL, not handwritten model classes.

docs.title: Create and discover tables
docs.text:
Select the application's database in S0ADM's database explorer. Install local authentication first, then execute the tracker schema. The auth user table must exist before the business foreign keys can be created. Run Introspect if the operation has not already refreshed models. Restart after external schema changes if introspection is unavailable.

The generated name capitalizes the table name: project becomes Project, task becomes Task, and soad_auth_user becomes Soad_auth_user. When a controller has the same name, alias the model:

from models import Project as ProjectModel

class Project(object):
    pass

Generated classes and database connections belong to the runtime. Do not check generated models into Git or introduce a separate ORM session.

docs.title: CRUD operations
docs.text:
from models import Project as ProjectModel

project = ProjectModel()
project.set("name", "Website launch")
project.set("owner_id", ctx.output["current_user"]["id"])
project.saveIt()

mine = ProjectModel.where("owner_id = ?", ctx.output["current_user"]["id"])
page = mine.orderBy("id DESC").limit(20).offset(0)
one = ProjectModel.first("id = ? AND owner_id = ?",
                         project.getId(), ctx.output["current_user"]["id"])
one.set("name", "Website launch v2")
one.saveIt()

Use first(condition, values...) for one match; do not call .first() on a LazyList. findById(id) works for a primary key, but private records should be loaded with an ownership condition too. Check for None before modifying a row. delete() deletes a loaded model; the tracker only exposes deletion through guarded POST actions.

docs.title: Inputs, search, and relationships
docs.text:
Bind values with ? parameters. Do not interpolate submitted values into SQL. SQL identifiers and sort expressions cannot be value parameters; select them from a fixed allowlist instead.

sorts = {"newest": "id DESC", "name": "name ASC, id ASC"}
sort = sorts.get(ctx.getParameter("sort"), sorts["newest"])
rows = ProjectModel.where("owner_id = ? AND name LIKE ?",
                          ctx.output["current_user"]["id"], "%launch%")
rows = rows.orderBy(sort).limit(20)

LIKE treats % and _ as wildcards; decide whether your search UI permits these patterns. Limit page sizes and use stable ordering. The tracker fetches 21 rows and displays 20 to determine whether a next page exists.

Use explicit foreign keys and indexes. When loading a task, authorize its parent project before reading or changing the task. A valid task ID does not prove the caller may access it.

docs.title: IDs, dates, and blobs
docs.text:
Use an auto-increment id for the tutorial and saveIt() for inserts/updates. If you deliberately use a manually assigned string/UUID primary key, use insert() for a new row and saveIt() for an existing row.

Prefer explicit created_date/updated_date columns if you want application control over timestamps. created_at and updated_at have ActiveJDBC-managed semantics; do not set those reserved timestamps manually.

The tracker has a separate attachment table to avoid loading blobs in list queries. Uploads are bounded and served through an authorized controller action; they are not public assets.

docs.title: Commit, rollback, and migrations
docs.text:
The engine opens a database transaction around dispatch and rendering, commits on success, and rolls back on exceptions. Validate all input before writing. Returning a validation view or calling sendError is not, by itself, an instruction to undo earlier writes. Do not suppress an exception after partial updates and assume they rolled back.

DDL may commit implicitly in MySQL. Keep migrations separate from web requests, back up first, apply each migration once, and regenerate models afterward. Reverting application source does not revert a database migration.

For SQL bundles and older IDE schemas, see migrations.

docs.title: 5. Transactions and routing
docs.text: A transaction is a Jython class loaded by its group and code. For tracker/project.py, the class name is Project. For address_book.py it is Address_book, not AddressBook.

docs.title: URL and action contract
Request and response context
docs.text:
API Use ctx.getRequest(), ctx.getResponse() Jakarta servlet request/response ctx.getParameter("name") Ordinary submitted parameter ctx.getHeader("HX-Request") Request header ctx.json() Parse JSON body to a map ctx.output Values available to the view ctx.output["current_user"] Authorized application identity ctx.ctxPath Framework routing prefix; preserve it in links ctx.go_to Redirect string or response callable ctx.page_layout = False Disable wrapper for fragments/JSON/downloads

render.as_view(ctx, "edit") returns a callable; assign it to ctx.go_to. Returning a value from an action is not the normal response mechanism. ctx.redirect(url) sets the redirect destination.

docs.title: Validation and response status
docs.text:
Trim text, enforce lengths, allowlist enumerations, and parse IDs before database access. On invalid input re-render the form with the submitted values and field feedback. HTML validation is convenience; the controller enforces the rules.

as_view sets status 200 when invoked. To return an HTML form with 400:

from utils import render

def _invalid_form(ctx):
    render_view = render.as_view(ctx, "edit")
    def response():
        html = render_view()
        ctx.getResponse().setStatus(400)
        return html
    ctx.go_to = response

For missing private records, return 404 without revealing who owns them. For invalid parameters use 400. A denied permission or invalid CSRF token gives 403; missing security setup gives 503. Always inspect response content and redirects when testing, not just whether a request completed.

Next: render forms and layouts.

docs.title: 6. Views and frontend development
docs.text: Views are Handlebars HTML templates. A transaction named tracker/project loads its views from tracker/_project/ at runtime.

docs.title: Template data
docs.text:
ctx.output["heading"] = "My projects"
ctx.output["projects"] = projects
ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "project")

<h1>{{heading}}</h1>
{{#each projects}}
  <a href="{{../ctxPath}}/t/tracker/project/edit?id={{id}}">{{name}}</a>
{{else}}
  <p>No projects yet. Create your first project.</p>
{{/each}}

{{value}} escapes HTML. Only mark framework-generated layout content or explicitly trusted HTML as safe; never render a user's name, description, or error with triple braces. Within each, use ../ to reach parent context.

The renderer supplies comparison helpers, select, option, ref_lookup, dateFmt, length, size, html, session, get, and i18n. See the rendering reference for signatures and limits.

docs.title: Shared page layout
docs.text:
A base transaction can provide a layout location that page transactions inherit:

class Layout(object):
    def page_layout(self, ctx):
        return ("tracker", "layout", "layout")

class Project(Layout):
    pass

The engine extracts the rendered document's body/head/title and combines them with the layout. The tracker layout uses {{body}} for the framework-supplied safe content, while normal template values remain escaped. The layout controller must implement view(ctx), even when it only contains pass; the engine invokes it to prepare layout data. The IDE policy audit requires both public methods on the base layout to be covered.

Use a complete document for pages; set ctx.page_layout = False for a fragment, JSON response, or download. Do not wrap JSON inside the site's HTML shell.

docs.title: Forms and navigation
docs.text:
<form method="post" action="{{ctxPath}}/t/tracker/project/save">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{csrf_token}}">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="{{project.id}}">
  <label for="name">Project name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" value="{{project.name}}" maxlength="120" required>
  {{#if error}}<p role="alert">{{error}}</p>{{/if}}
  <button type="submit">Save project</button>
</form>

Successful POST actions redirect to a GET page, avoiding duplicate writes on refresh. Include visible labels, keyboard focus, readable contrast, a viewport meta tag, and useful empty states. Use a horizontally scrollable wrapper for tables on small screens.

docs.title: Tailwind and assets
docs.text:
The tracker includes a Tailwind input stylesheet and a small dependency manifest. Build its CSS before uploading webapp/assets/tracker/tracker.css; see the example setup. Serve compiled assets locally, without the Tailwind browser CDN in production.

Your application owns its assets. S0ADM's component classes and asset routes are IDE implementation details and are absent from the production application image. When extending S0ADM itself, follow its existing Tailwind component layer and rebuild its committed stylesheet.

docs.title: Progressive enhancement
docs.text:
Ordinary forms work without JavaScript. To add htmx, package its reviewed script in your application assets, then attach attributes:

<form hx-post="{{ctxPath}}/t/tracker/project/save"
      hx-target="#project-panel" method="post"
      action="{{ctxPath}}/t/tracker/project/save">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{csrf_token}}">
  <!-- The same labeled inputs as the ordinary form. -->
</form>

Provide a controller response appropriate for both modes: an HTML fragment with layout disabled for htmx, or the normal redirect for a full form submission. The downloadable tracker uses ordinary forms throughout, so enhancement is optional rather than a prerequisite.

docs.title: 7. Build the project/task tracker
docs.text: This chapter connects the database, transaction, and view concepts into one application. The complete source is included so you can compare your work at each stage.

docs.title: 1. Prepare identity and data
docs.text:
Complete the setup, then configure the five permissions and grants in the plan. Install schema.sql in the application's database and run Introspect. The Project, Task, Attachment, and Soad_auth_user models must be available before the controllers import them.

Create transactions in this order:

Group/code Controller Views tracker/layout Layout layout.html tracker/project Project project.html, edit.html tracker/task Task task.html, edit.html

Copy their contents from the example's webapp/WEB-INF/jython/default/tracker/ directory. For the CLI use soad create and then place source in the nested CLI layout described in chapter 12.

docs.title: 2. Create and list projects
docs.text:
Project.view reads only rows whose owner_id equals ctx.output["current_user"]["id"]. Its query binds the search value and limits results to 20 plus one look-ahead row.

Project.save trims and checks the name before writing. A new project's owner is taken from the authenticated context, never from a hidden form field. An existing project is loaded with both its ID and owner ID.

Open /t/tracker/project, create “Website launch”, and confirm it appears. Edit its name. Submit an empty name with browser validation bypassed and verify the controller returns feedback without creating a row.

docs.title: 3. Add tasks and assignment
docs.text:
Task imports the project's private ownership helpers. Every task action loads the requested project through that ownership check before loading a task. A task is then looked up by both id and project_id, preventing a caller from combining their project ID with somebody else's task ID.

Create “Write homepage”, assign an active application user, and change its status through todo, doing, and done. The server rejects any other status and rejects nonexistent or disabled assignees. The assignee selector passes only ID and display name to the view, not entire authentication records.

Invite a second application user through /_soad/auth/admin/users to populate the selector. Assignment is a label, not project membership.

docs.title: 4. Add presentation and navigation
docs.text:
Build and upload the example's CSS as described in its README. The layout provides navigation, profile/sign-out links, a skip link, and a content area. Forms preserve submitted values on errors. Tables scroll on narrow screens.

Set the default application's Welcome transaction to tracker/project in System Settings. Its persisted release setting is WEB-INF/sufia-app.properties; an operator's sufia_welcome_transaction environment override takes precedence.

docs.title: 5. Add attachments and JSON
docs.text:
Upload a small text file while saving a task. Download it through the task's authorized download action. Removing or replacing an attachment happens within the database transaction. The example deliberately serves bytes as an attachment, with application/octet-stream and nosniff.

Visit:

/t/tracker/task/data?project_id=PROJECT_ID

You should receive a JSON object containing a bounded task list, page number, and has_next. This endpoint uses the same login and ownership rules as HTML; it does not automatically become a bearer-token API.

docs.title: 6. Prove the access rules
docs.text:
Use two separate browser sessions. Create a project as user A; sign in as member B and request A's project edit URL, task URLs, and attachment URL. Each must deny access without returning A's data.

As a member, POSTing project deletion should return 403 even for your own project. As an administrator, deletion of your own project succeeds and cascades to tasks/attachments. An administrator still cannot delete somebody else's project through this tutorial's routes.

The delete controls disclose the action and consequence before the final submit. The server policy is authoritative even when a control is visible.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: You now have a complete CRUD application with separate accounts, data ownership, roles, assignment, filtering, pagination, uploads, and JSON output. Run the acceptance checks before following the deployment chapters. Team sharing, notifications, and optimistic concurrency are deliberate extension exercises, not hidden requirements of the supplied implementation.

docs.title: 8. Built-in authentication: use, configure, and override
docs.text: SØAD supplies application-local login and authorization. The application's users, roles, permissions, tokens, and revocable sessions live in its own datasource. An S0ADM login does not authenticate a user to your web application.

docs.title: Choose a mode
docs.text:
Profile / mode Use authenticated / local Protected application using built-in accounts mixed / local Public pages plus protected actions public / public Entirely public application, without a login provider authenticated or mixed / custom Your provider owns identity and authentication

The security manifest at WEB-INF/security/app-security.json defines the application's mode, roles, permission grants, and registration policy. Changing a controller policy does not register its permission automatically.

flowchart TD
    Request --> Manifest{Security metadata ready?}
    Manifest -->|No| Unavailable[503]
    Manifest -->|Yes| Policy{Action policy}
    Policy -->|Missing| Denied[403]
    Policy -->|Public| Action[Run action]
    Policy -->|Protected| Identity{Signed in?}
    Identity -->|No| Login[Login redirect]
    Identity -->|Yes| Checks[Check CSRF for mutation and permission]
    Checks -->|Denied| Denied
    Checks -->|Allowed| Owner[Application ownership validation]
    Owner --> Action

docs.title: Set up the built-in provider
docs.text:
1. Open System Settings → Applications → your application as an IDE superadmin.
  2. Initialize the Security card with authenticated, local identity, and roles admin and member. Save and follow the one-time application-password link.
  3. Open that application's Roles and permissions section. Add the codes from the tracker plan and select their grants. Save to publish the manifest and install matching development metadata.
  4. Keep registration invite_only for this tutorial. Open registration requires a least-privilege member role and must not grant administrator access.
  5. Test an application route with the new application account.

Initial role setup and later permission editing are different forms. The platform-level Roles screen controls IDE access; it is not the application's permission editor. An unregistered permission:code denies every user; inspect the application's policy audit and logs if even an administrator receives 403.

docs.title: Protect controllers and records
docs.text:
class Project(object):
    ACCESS_POLICY = {
        "view": "permission:projects.read",
        "save": "permission:projects.write",
        "delete": "permission:projects.delete",
    }

Use public, authenticated, or permission:<registered-code> for each action. Set POST/PUT/DELETE method docstrings on mutations. Authenticated local mutations accept the csrf_token form field or CSRF-Token request header. For JSON, put the token in the header, not only inside the JSON body.

Public local-auth actions receive a token in the template context, but the business action must validate CSRF itself for public state changes. The runtime's protected-action check does not make public writes safe automatically.

Policies decide whether a caller may run an action. Your query must still enforce record ownership, organization membership, or other business access rules.

docs.title: Built-in pages and settings
docs.text:
Route under /_soad/auth Purpose /login, /logout Sign in and sign out /bootstrap First administrator setup, gated by absence of an active admin /register Self-registration when enabled /forgot, /reset Password recovery /invite Invitation and initial password setup /profile, /password Profile/password management /totp/setup TOTP enrollment/removal /sessions List/revoke sessions /admin/users Account creation, invitations, status, roles /health Manifest/schema readiness

Create the first production admin with soad-auth-admin before exposing the service, or complete the bootstrap page on a restricted setup connection. Browser bootstrap grants system_admin; use its user administration page to grant the business admin role afterward. The administrative CLI also grants the manifest's generated owner/admin role. Use invitation setup links as secrets. Password resets and account disabling revoke active sessions. TOTP is implemented; do not describe it as future work.

Configure sufia_hostname as the public HTTPS origin and sufia_app_name as the display name. SMTP uses mail_smtp_host, mail_smtp_port, mail_smtp_username, mail_smtp_password, and mail_sender_email. See the mail transport limitation in integrations.

The checked-in production profile has session.cookie.secure=true, session.cookie.httponly=true, session.cookie.samesite=NONE, and a 1,800-second idle timeout. This guide's same-site tracker deployments explicitly choose LAX; keep NONE only when your cross-site flow needs it and always use HTTPS. The local auth session record also has its own expiry; changing the servlet idle timeout does not change that database session lifetime.

docs.title: Override appearance without replacing authentication
docs.text:
Put validated templates under WEB-INF/auth-overrides/; shared CSS belongs at assets/auth-overrides/auth.css. Start with login.html, and retain its field names, action URLs, CSRF field, and required page structure.

A template is not an ordinary application view: the override validator permits only its supported template/markup contract. Do not reuse the tracker layout or load a CDN. Use the full screen-by-screen contract for the exact required inputs and context for every screen, including bootstrap.

Override mark.svg to replace the small-screen logo. Missing or invalid templates/styles/marks fall back to the bundled UI and log the reason. Removing an override restores the default. Presentation overrides do not change password, session, or permission verification.

docs.title: Replace authentication behavior
docs.text:
Choose Custom application provider and a lowercase module such as security/auth_provider. Its Auth_provider class must implement:

Method Contract current_user(ctx) Current identity or None authenticate(ctx) Authenticated identity or None authorize(ctx, action, permission) Exactly True to grant the permission validate_csrf(ctx) Exactly True to accept a protected mutation login_url(ctx), logout_url(ctx) URLs for your authentication flow

The provider module is not directly routable. Put login/callback actions in separate transactions with explicit policies. A custom provider must supply credential verification or a complete external identity integration, session handling, revocation, callback/return validation, and CSRF behavior. Selecting custom does not install OIDC or SSO automatically.

See the provider skeleton and fail-closed rules. The skeleton deliberately grants nothing until implemented. After changing modes, publish matching metadata/SQL and test before deploying. Keep old local tables during an initial rollback window; the runtime does not drop them automatically.

Transaction-owned auth pages are an advanced local-provider integration, distinct from templates and custom providers. Their route mapping must be registered in the manifest; do not implement a second password store or assume the archived roadmap is a current API contract.

docs.title: 9. Files, APIs, and integrations
docs.text: Add integrations after the main CRUD flow and its access rules work.

docs.title: Upload and download
docs.text:
Use enctype="multipart/form-data" and a named file input. The framework's request wrapper exposes an UploadedFile through getParameter:

upload = ctx.getRequest().getParameter("attachment")
if upload:
    filename = upload.getFileName()
    size = upload.getSize()
    content = upload.getBytes()       # only for a deliberately bounded small file

It also supports getInputStream() and writeTo(destination). The wrapper must be accessed through ctx.getRequest() for files: the convenience ctx.getParameter() has a Java String return type and cannot return UploadedFile. The wrapper provides <field>_fn and <field>_ft metadata. Empty uploads are falsey. Do not call multipart parsing again inside the controller. Temporary files are cleaned when request processing finishes; copy or consume them during the action.

Configure max.file.upload.size, max.request.upload.size, and optionally file.upload.temp.dir. Oversized requests return 413. The tracker adds a 1 MiB application limit and sanitizes the download filename; it never uses the submitted name as a filesystem path.

The tracker reads an attachment only after checking project ownership and the task's project membership. It sets attachment=True, an opaque content type, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. It does not scan malware or make uploaded content safe to execute. Add scanning/quarantine if your application's use requires it.

For large files use bounded streaming and private storage with generated keys. If a filesystem write accompanies a database update, define cleanup/retry behavior explicitly: database rollback does not remove the file.

docs.title: JSON and AJAX
docs.text:
ctx.page_layout = False
ctx.go_to = render.as_json(ctx, {"ok": True, "project_id": project.getId()})

Pass a deliberately selected object. Calling as_json(ctx) without one serializes all output, which may include identity and CSRF context unsuitable for the endpoint. Never serialize whole auth models.

Use ctx.json() for request JSON and validate keys/types before updates. Cookie-authenticated AJAX must carry cookies and the CSRF-Token header on protected writes. A login redirect is not a JSON success response; clients should detect expired authentication and navigate to sign-in.

The framework does not infer CORS, bearer authentication, or an API versioning scheme from a JSON response. Design those requirements explicitly with filters and/or a custom provider.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
The bundled mail utility is from utils import mailer. Its concrete entrypoints are listed in rendering and utilities. Set mail configuration through environment variables and restart after changes; the utility establishes configuration at module load.

Use a test relay before enabling account recovery in production. Confirm sender identity, public HTTPS links, and delivery with your mail operator. The current bundled SMTP helper explicitly trusts all TLS certificates on its STARTTLS path. It should not be described as certificate-verified transport; use a controlled relay/network boundary or remediate the mail transport before relying on it across an untrusted network.

Do not send email inside a request and assume database rollback can recall it. For reliable notifications, persist an outbox entry in the transaction and have an external worker deliver/retry it. SØAD does not automatically provision that worker.

docs.title: Reports and external services
docs.text:
render.as_pdf renders a Handlebars view through the bundled PDF converter. Use a report-specific, simple HTML/CSS template rather than expecting browser JavaScript or a full Tailwind layout to print identically.

Apache POI can generate Excel workbooks. Use server-generated filenames and the file/blob renderers for downloads. Escape spreadsheet formula-leading user text when exporting untrusted strings.

Java's HTTP client can call external services from Jython. Set connection/request timeouts, validate response status, keep keys in environment-backed configuration, and decide whether failure should abort the business update or be retried later. CPython libraries such as requests are not part of this runtime.

docs.title: 10. Filters, errors, and logging
docs.text: Use filters for request-wide behavior, controller policies for action access, and business queries for record ownership.

docs.title: Transaction filters
docs.text:
Create a transaction under the reserved default/filter/ group with the capitalized class and all three lifecycle methods:

class Headers(object):
    url_mapping = "/t/*"

    def filter_init(self, config):
        pass

    def do_filter(self, request, response, chain):
        response.setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
        chain.doFilter(request, response)

    def destroy(self):
        pass

Call the chain exactly once to continue; omit it only when completing the response yourself. Filters are shared across requests, so do not store a user, request, or database connection on self.

flowchart TD
    Request --> FilterA[First filter before]
    FilterA --> FilterB[Second filter before]
    FilterB --> Servlet
    Servlet --> ReturnB[Second filter after]
    ReturnB --> ReturnA[First filter after]
    ReturnA --> Response

Discovery/instances are cached: restart after adding, removing, renaming, or editing a filter. The default-app filter group is the discovery source, not one independent group per datasource. See the filter reference for exact ordering, wildcard mappings, scope exclusions, and failure behavior.

docs.title: Error pages
docs.text:
The framework has separate defaults for missing resources (404), explicit 500 errors, and uncaught exceptions. Optional default-app transactions are:

Code Template errors/err404 errors/_err404/err404.html errors/err500 errors/_err500/err500.html errors/errexc errors/_errexc/errexc.html

Error override view(ctx) runs in a special lifecycle: no normal auth, application filter, database transaction, or page layout. Keep it independent of the database so it works during outages. IDE and internal routes use bundled pages rather than business overrides.

The original status is retained, even when a renderer sets 200. An invalid override falls back to the bundled error page. ctx.getError() exposes details only during error dispatch; those details are not automatically displayed. See the full error contract.

docs.title: Logs and diagnosis
docs.text:
from sufia.util import Log
Log.info(ctx, "Project save completed")

Use the IDE log viewer in development and container stdout/stderr for deployed applications. Do not log passwords, setup/reset links, session cookies, provider keys, or uploaded contents.

The development mode can log request and session information and reloads transaction modules. Use sufia.mode=production in production. An unexplained 404 may be an import failure; inspect the accompanying log before changing routing. A 503 on protected routes often means authentication schema/manifest mismatch rather than a controller exception.

docs.title: 11. S0ADM features, including AI
docs.text: S0ADM is the browser development environment for SØAD. Use it to create and test applications, manage development metadata, and prepare releases. Keep it on a restricted development/control-plane instance.

docs.title: Workspace and application tools
docs.text:
Feature Developer workflow Applications/settings Select/configure apps, developer access, security, welcome route Transaction editor Create group/code, edit Jython and views, save/compile, preview Editor workspace Open multiple transactions/files, switch tabs, retain drafts Versions Inspect prior transaction saves and restore a selected version File manager Browse folders, create/upload/rename/edit/download application files Database explorer Inspect schema, tables/columns, records, DDL, query results SQL editor Execute reviewed SQL, inspect history/results, refresh generated models Logs Diagnose compile/runtime/database errors People and profile IDE users/roles, access, profile, sessions, and account security Gallery Discover/import packaged application content where configured Release/deployment Prepare an application image and view build progress

Saving transaction source is not the same as applying database DDL. When adding a column, update the schema, refresh models, then save the controller and template. Unsaved editor drafts are not deployed source; check the saved version before export or release.

System settings and deployment actions require elevated IDE privileges. Features also depend on the image, license, datasource, and installed tools. The deployment screen reports unavailable builds when Kaniko is absent; a standalone image does not imply in-cluster builds are enabled.

docs.title: Configure the AI assistant
docs.text:
As superadmin, open System Settings → Applications → an application → AI assistant. Configure provider family, endpoint, API key, model, and enabled state. These settings are platform-wide, even when reached from one application's page.

Supported wire families are OpenAI-compatible chat completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic messages. Use a model available from your configured provider; the guide does not pin a changing provider model catalog.

Property Environment variable ai.enabled ai_enabled ai.provider ai_provider ai.endpoint ai_endpoint ai.api.key ai_api_key ai.model ai_model ai.auto.accept ai_auto_accept

Resolution is per field: saved IDE settings, then environment, properties, and built-in default. Auto-accept defaults off. Restart for property/environment changes. Keep secrets in managed configuration rather than pasted application code.

docs.title: Understand the two AI workflows
docs.text:
Transaction editor chat: open a transaction and choose AI/Edit with AI. Ask it to read code, diagnose logs, propose changes, or restore versions. Ordinary source edits are staged for diff review; Approve & Execute publishes them. Auto-accept can automate eligible approvals when enabled.

Dashboard whole-app generation: describe a complete app on a suitable empty application. This has a separate server-authorized workflow: it can execute SQL, install provisional transactions, review and validate them, and publish the result. Do not assume that no database or source changes occur before final publication. Follow the visible workflow state and use a disposable development database for a first attempt.

flowchart TD
    Prompt --> Mode{Development workflow}
    Mode -->|Editor chat| Read[Read source and schema]
    Read --> Stage[Stage changes and show diff]
    Stage --> Approval[Manual approval or enabled auto-accept]
    Approval --> Save[Save changes]
    Mode -->|Whole-app generation| Plan[Prepare app and security plan]
    Plan --> Build[Authorized schema and provisional source changes]
    Build --> Validate[Review and runtime validation]
    Validate --> Publish[Publish or report failure]

Normal chat SQL blocks have an Execute action for the developer. Rename/move is an immediate tool operation with conversational confirmation semantics; check internal links afterward. These are different from staged file editing. See AI workflows for details.

docs.title: A useful tracker prompt
docs.text:
Build an authenticated project/task tracker using local application identity. Members own projects and may manage tasks in their own projects. Assignment does not grant access. Register projects.read, projects.write, tasks.read, tasks.write for admin/member, and projects.delete for admin. Check ownership on HTML, JSON, and download actions. Use Jython 2.7, Handlebars, and local compiled Tailwind assets. Show the schema and review the access rules.

For larger work, use the planning guide to create a schema, route/action list, acceptance criteria, and phases before generation. Project AGENTS.md conventions help preserve naming and design choices.

Review generated SQL, permissions, uploads, and business validations just as you would review manually written code. Model output and runtime validation are not a substitute for testing with different user accounts.

docs.title: 12. SOAD CLI and local agent workflows
docs.text: The SOAD CLI lets you use a local editor while synchronizing transactions with an S0ADM server. It does not run the Java server, execute schema migrations, or turn a source sync into a complete production release.

docs.title: Install and authenticate
docs.text:
Obtain the CLI from your SØAD distribution. The checked installer targets Webgeaz-Sdn-Bhd releases; older documentation refers to webgeaz/soadcli. Release access could not be verified publicly during this consolidation; use the release/installer supplied with your installation if a repository requires access.

The installer expects archives named soadcli_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz, containing a soad executable. macOS uses darwin, Linux uses linux, Apple Silicon uses arm64, and x86-64 uses amd64. After downloading and extracting the matching archive, a user-local installation is:

mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
install -m 755 /path/to/extracted/soad "$HOME/.local/bin/soad"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Add that PATH entry to your shell startup configuration to retain it. The shipped shell installer instead installs into /usr/local/bin using sudo; inspect it before running it. Native Windows packaging is not verified by this guide; use a supported Linux environment such as WSL with the appropriate binary.

soad version
soad --help
mkdir tracker-workspace
cd tracker-workspace
soad login --server https://ide.example.com
soad list

Interactive login saves project configuration and credentials in .config.json. Keep it out of Git, release archives, and agent prompts. Use separate project directories for development and production connections. For noninteractive login, the verified CLI supports SOAD_LOGIN and SOAD_PASSWORD, or SOAD_API_KEY and SOAD_APP_ID; inject them from your secret manager instead of command arguments.

The examples were checked against the installed CLI help (commit 5342396). Use soad COMMAND --help to confirm flags in another version.

docs.title: Local and runtime paths
docs.text:
File CLI workspace Runtime under WEB-INF/jython/default Controller src/tracker/project/project.py tracker/project.py View src/tracker/project/_project/edit.html tracker/_project/edit.html

Do not copy the extra per-transaction CLI directory directly into runtime routing. The CLI's checksum file tracks local changes, but is not a database migration ledger or a source-control history.

docs.title: Daily development
docs.text:
soad create tracker/project
# Edit the scaffolded controller and views in your editor.
soad changed
soad compare tracker/project
soad push tracker/project

For an existing transaction, pull before starting work:

soad pull tracker/project

Preserve any unpushed local edits before pulling. Coordinate with other developers and compare against the current server before pushing; do not assume automatic semantic merging.

Command Use pull --all Download all transactions push-all Upload all locally changed transactions push tracker/project --zip Alternative upload when a WAF blocks the usual request release --version v1.0 --notes "Tracker baseline" Create server source snapshot release --list List snapshots rollback --version v1.0 Restore a source snapshot deploy TARGET_FOLDER Copy source into runtime layout under a target directory delete tracker/project Delete remote and local transaction clean Delete the local src tree

Quote wildcard arguments such as 'tracker/*' so the shell does not expand them. Confirm push-remote arguments with its help before using another server. Source rollback does not restore database rows/schema. deploy requires a target folder and does not create auth SQL, install assets, or roll out Kubernetes.

docs.title: Use another agent harness with the SOAD skill
docs.text:
The CLI distribution's source bundle includes soad-ai-context/soad-framework/SKILL.md and a reference/ directory. Install the whole folder, not only the main Markdown file. The skill is a guide for writing SØAD code; the soad executable performs synchronization.

Different harnesses discover skills differently. Use your harness's documented skill-directory/import mechanism, then ask it to load soad-framework for the workspace. If the harness has no skill loader, explicitly give it the main SKILL.md and the referenced files relevant to the task. This does not require the IDE's built-in AI provider.

Before the first write, ask the agent to confirm:

  • It loaded the skill and recognizes Jython 2.7, generated models, and the CLI layout.
  • It knows the selected development application without printing its credentials.
  • It will create/pull, edit, compare, and push only the transactions in your task.
  • It will keep SQL in migration files for your chosen database execution workflow.
  • It will not treat delete, clean, release, rollback, or deployment as ordinary saves.

Example request:

Load the installed soad-framework skill. In this development workspace, pull tracker/task, add a status filter using parameterized queries, preserve ACCESS_POLICY and ownership checks, show the diff, then push the approved change. Do not modify schema or publish a release.

Older skill bundles may contain obsolete authentication or rendering examples. Use this repository's contracts when they disagree, and update the bundle. After pushing, test the real application session and expected response content; an IDE API token does not authenticate a browser to the runtime application.

docs.title: 13. Testing and completing the application
docs.text: Test behavior at the boundary where it matters. A successful compile or HTTP 200 does not prove that a protected application works correctly.

docs.title: Test layers
docs.text:
Layer What to verify Pure validation Lengths, identifiers, allowed status values Jython and database Generated models, queries, ownership, cascades, rollback HTTP Routing, method guards, authorization, CSRF, redirects, content type Browser Forms, errors, saved values, downloads, narrow-screen usability Deployment Image content, installed schema/manifest, readiness, persistence

The tracker includes an isolated JVM/H2 test script. See its README for the command and exactly which boundaries it covers.

Framework-maintainer checks from this repository:

./dev.sh test

These are offline JUnit/Jython checks with H2. Browser integration uses ./dev.sh test-ide-ui; test-ide-all also runs HTTP smoke checks. Those commands need the container/browser environment and test the IDE, not automatically every application you create.

docs.title: Tracker acceptance checklist
docs.text:
1. Anonymous requests redirect to application login; an IDE session alone is insufficient.
  2. Admin and member accounts can create/edit their own projects and tasks.
  3. Invalid name/title/status produces feedback and no partial update.
  4. IDs for another owner are rejected on list details, edit, save, delete, JSON, and download paths; a task cannot be moved by submitting another project ID.
  5. A member cannot invoke the project-delete route. Administrator access still obeys ownership.
  6. Missing/incorrect CSRF tokens fail on protected mutations. GET requests to save/delete do not change data.
  7. Pagination is stable; filtering stays active when moving between pages.
  8. A disabled/nonexistent assignee is rejected. Assignment alone grants no access.
  9. Small uploads download as attachments; oversize uploads fail; replacement, removal, task deletion, and project deletion remove the expected blob rows.
  10. HTML-like titles display as text; quotes/newlines in filenames do not create response headers. JSON contains only selected fields.
  11. Failed login, logout, reset, and revoked sessions behave correctly. Test recovery email and TOTP with disposable accounts.
  12. After restart, database records remain; session persistence follows the deployment's configured storage and expiry.

docs.title: Before release
docs.text:
Record the framework/CLI version, application source version, business migration version, image digest, and security manifest checksum together. Back up the application database and test restoration. Apply SQL only to the intended environment. Confirm the runtime contains no IDE directory, IDE database, development account credentials, or provider API keys.

Use production mode, HTTPS, secure cookies, configured public origin, and bounded upload settings. Exercise /_soad/auth/health and a real protected page after installing auth SQL.

docs.title: Failure and rollback
docs.text:
A source rollback is not a database restore. If a deployment changes auth metadata, old and new manifests may not both match the installed checksum. Plan a maintenance window or an explicitly compatible migration; the example's single-replica deployment uses Recreate and permits downtime.

For a failed rollout, restore a known image and its compatible metadata/schema. Never rerun an initial business CREATE TABLE script against a populated database as a substitute for a migration.

docs.title: 14. Deploy with Docker
docs.text: Build an application-only image, install its database bundles, and create an application administrator. S0ADM belongs on the development instance.

docs.title: Prepare an immutable application release
docs.text:
The tutorial's preparation script creates a fresh release/ containing only its source, built CSS, welcome configuration, security manifest, and SQL bundles. It does not export live users or copy the IDE database.

For your own app, use S0ADM's release preparation where available or construct an equivalent reviewed build context. The CLI's deploy TARGET_FOLDER only rearranges transaction source; separately include your assets, application libraries, welcome configuration, auth overrides, manifest, and SQL bundles. Do not copy the entire IDE webapp/ directory into an application image.

flowchart LR
    Source[Reviewed application source and assets] --> Context[Release context]
    Policy[Security plan] --> Manifest[Manifest and auth SQL]
    Manifest --> Context
    Context --> Image[Application image]
    Manifest --> Database[(Production database)]
    Image --> Runtime
    Runtime --> Database

From the repository root, after building the tracker CSS:

./dev.sh build
java -cp 'app/lib/*' org.python.util.jython -B \
  docs/examples/tracker/tools/prepare.py docs/examples/tracker/release
docker build -f app/Dockerfile-base-runtime -t soad-runtime:tracker app
docker build --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=soad-runtime:tracker \
  -t tracker:1.0 docs/examples/tracker/release

The base uses Java 21 and contains server/ and soad-auth-admin; it omits s0adm/. The application Dockerfile writes webapp/ through /opt/sufia/webapp/, the target of the base's /app/webapp symlink. Keep the base/application versions coupled; use a private registry and immutable tags or digests for your releases.

docs.title: Local container rehearsal
docs.text:
The Compose example is deliberately a localhost HTTP rehearsal, with an isolated MySQL database. Supply TRACKER_DB_PASSWORD and TRACKER_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD through your shell's secret input mechanism or an untracked .env file in the example directory. Do not commit that file.

cd docs/examples/tracker
docker compose up -d db
docker compose exec db mysql --user=root --password --database=tracker \
  -e "source /install/auth-mysql.sql; source /install/tracker.sql;"
docker compose up -d tracker
docker compose exec tracker soad-auth-admin create-admin \
  --app default --email admin@example.com --name "Tracker Administrator" --password-stdin

Enter the initial application password on stdin when requested by the command. For automated use, pipe a mounted secret file into docker compose exec -T instead. Do not pass a password argument.

Open http://localhost:8081/_soad/auth/login, then /t/tracker/project. Readiness should return 200:

curl --fail http://localhost:8081/_soad/auth/health
docker compose logs --tail=100 tracker

The initial SQL commands are for a fresh database only. For subsequent releases apply reviewed migrations and the release's matching auth metadata bundle. docker compose down preserves the named database volume; adding --volumes would delete it. Local container sessions may be lost on container replacement.

docs.title: Production configuration
docs.text:
Use an external or properly managed database, database credentials from your secret manager, a TLS reverse proxy, and a public origin:

sufia_hostname=https://tracker.example.com
sufia_app_name=Project Tracker
session_cookie_secure=true
session_cookie_samesite=LAX
db_default_driver_class=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
db_default_url=jdbc:mysql://db.example.internal:3306/tracker?sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY

The database server's certificate chain must be trusted by the JVM for VERIFY_IDENTITY. The local Compose JDBC URL disables TLS solely for its isolated rehearsal network; do not copy it to an untrusted database connection.

Set database username/password separately, configure SMTP if using recovery emails, and provide writable directories for generated models, logs, upload temporaries, and session storage. Persist business data in the database. The tracker stores attachments there too.

docs.title: Upgrade and recover
docs.text:
Back up before migrations, retain the prior image digest, and install matching auth SQL before routing traffic to the new runtime. A checksum mismatch causes 503 readiness/access failure. A changed manifest can also make the old image unready, so coordinate metadata updates and image replacement.

Use container logs and health checks for diagnostics. The application-only image does not expose S0ADM's log viewer, file editor, or AI service.

docs.title: 15. Deploy with Kubernetes
docs.text: The example manifest deploys one tracker replica with a Service, TLS Ingress, configuration, and a session PVC. It assumes an existing MySQL database and an installed Ingress controller.

docs.title: Prepare the cluster inputs
docs.text:
1. Build/push the application image from chapter 14.
  2. Create the application database and apply the release's auth SQL and business migrations using your normal database administration connection.
  3. Replace the example image, database hostname, public hostname, Ingress class, and resource/storage settings. Supply imagePullSecrets if the registry needs it.
  4. Create a TLS Secret named tracker-tls, or configure your certificate manager to create it. Point the public DNS record at the Ingress endpoint.
  5. Create the database Secret. The password file below must be a protected local file containing only the database password (without a trailing newline).
kubectl create namespace tracker
kubectl -n tracker create secret generic tracker-db \
  --from-file=password=/secure/path/tracker-db-password
kubectl -n tracker apply --dry-run=server -f docs/examples/tracker/kubernetes.yaml
kubectl -n tracker apply -f docs/examples/tracker/kubernetes.yaml
kubectl -n tracker rollout status deployment/tracker

These commands act on the current kubectl context. Check it before applying. The example expects a default dynamic storage class; otherwise specify one on the PVC. Protect/limit Secret access with your cluster's RBAC and secret system.

docs.title: Traffic and readiness
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Browser -->|HTTPS| Ingress
    Ingress --> Service
    Service --> Pod[Tracker runtime pod]
    Pod -->|JDBC| DB[(MySQL)]
    Config[ConfigMap and Secret] --> Pod
    Pod --> Sessions[(Session PVC)]

Startup/liveness use a TCP check for the JVM listener. Readiness uses /_soad/auth/health, which verifies auth schema/manifest compatibility and may fail during a database outage. Keeping database readiness separate from process liveness avoids restarting the JVM repeatedly for a database failure. See the Kubernetes probe guidance.

The auth health route is not a complete business-schema diagnostic. Also smoke test the application and inspect logs after rollout.

docs.title: Initialize and verify
docs.text:
Create the first administrator on stdin before opening access to the Ingress:

kubectl -n tracker exec -i deploy/tracker -- soad-auth-admin create-admin \
  --app default --email admin@example.com --name "Tracker Administrator" \
  --password-stdin < /secure/path/initial-admin-password
kubectl -n tracker logs deploy/tracker --tail=100
kubectl -n tracker get pods,pvc,svc,ingress

The stdin file is a temporary operator secret, not an image input. Check HTTPS sign-in, cookie behavior, project creation, and a private download. Confirm /s0adm/ is unavailable.

docs.title: Storage and scaling
docs.text:
The runtime generates model classes inside the application's writable filesystem. This example does not set a read-only root filesystem. It runs as UID/GID 1000 and uses fsGroup for the session volume.

Jetty's session store is file-based under the JVM temporary directory's s0-session-store. The example persists that path for a single replica. The database also contains revocable application session records; those records alone do not make servlet sessions distributed.

Do not raise replicas and assume shared login state. Multi-replica operation requires an explicitly designed servlet-session strategy, storage semantics, and testing; sticky routing alone does not provide failover. The example uses Recreate so two versions do not compete for a ReadWriteOnce volume. This introduces deployment downtime.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Set CPU/memory requests and limits from measurements; the sample values are a starting point. Monitor readiness, HTTP errors, latency, JVM memory, pool exhaustion, database capacity, and persistent volume usage.

Back up MySQL and verify restore procedures. Retain application image digests, auth SQL, manifests, and migration history. kubectl rollout undo rolls back the Deployment specification, not database state or a changed ConfigMap. Restore compatible metadata/configuration as part of the same recovery plan.

The manifest has been supplied as a template; cluster-specific admission, storage, TLS, and database behavior must be verified in your environment.

docs.title: 16. Put this documentation online
docs.text: The Markdown under docs/ is the source of truth. The repository's mkdocs.yml builds a static website with Material for MkDocs, chapter navigation, search, code highlighting, and Mermaid diagrams.

docs.title: Preview and build
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
.venv-docs/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. On Windows use the virtual environment's Scripts directory in place of bin. The docs tooling uses Python 3; this is independent of application Jython 2.7. See Material installation for platform alternatives.

Build and validate:

.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs build --strict

The resulting site/ directory is the deployable website. Do not host mkdocs serve as a production service. Before publishing, set site_url in mkdocs.yml to the final URL, including a path prefix if applicable, for example https://docs.example.com/soad/.

docs.title: Option A: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
Put the documentation repository on GitHub, enable Pages in repository Settings, and use a dedicated gh-pages branch as the publishing source. From an authorized checkout with Git push access:

.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs gh-deploy

This builds the site and pushes its generated contents to the publication branch. It does not deploy your SØAD application. For a private source repository, confirm your GitHub plan's Pages visibility and access rules before publishing.

For automatic publication, adapt the optional workflow below and save it as .github/workflows/docs.yml only when you want pushes to publish:

name: Publish documentation
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["docs/**", "mkdocs.yml", "requirements-docs.txt"]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - run: mkdocs gh-deploy

Change main to your actual publication branch and review action versions/pins under your organization's CI policy. This example is documentation, not an enabled workflow. See Material's publishing guide for the host setup.

docs.title: Option B: any static web host
docs.text:
Upload the contents of site/ to your static host's document root, bucket, or artifact deployment. Configure HTTPS, directory index support, and the base path corresponding to site_url. For a managed build service:

Setting Value Install python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt Build mkdocs build --strict Output site

With an existing web server, serve the generated HTML/assets as ordinary files. Do not expose the repository root, .git, runtime configuration, or databases. For a custom domain configure the host's domain binding, DNS, and TLS certificate.

docs.title: Diagrams, search, and offline environments
docs.text:
Mermaid fences render through the theme's diagram integration. Diagram JavaScript may need network access in a browser. For an air-gapped host, package a reviewed local Mermaid asset and configure local loading, or pre-render diagrams to SVG as part of your site's build. Test actual deployment CSP/network rules; a successful Markdown build alone does not prove diagrams render.

Open the hosted site over HTTP(S), not just as file:// pages, to test search and asset loading. Text beside each diagram explains the same relationship for readers whose renderer does not support Mermaid.

docs.title: Maintain the chapters

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
from urllib import quote
from models import Project as ProjectModel
from utils import render
from default.tracker.layout import Layout


def _id(value):
    value = str(value or "")
    if not value.isdigit() or len(value) > 10:
        return None
    result = int(value)
    return result if 0 < result <= 2147483647 else None


def _fail(ctx, status, message):
    ctx.page_layout = False
    ctx.go_to = render.as_string(ctx, message)


def _project(ctx, value):
    identity = _id(value)
    row = (ProjectModel.first("id = ? AND owner_id = ?", identity,
                              ctx.output["current_user"]["id"])
           if identity else None)
    if row is None:
        _fail(ctx, 404, "Project not found")
    return row


def _page(ctx):
    return min(_id(ctx.getParameter("page")) or 1, 10000)


class Project(Layout):
    ACCESS_POLICY = {
        "view": "permission:projects.read",
        "edit": "permission:projects.write",
        "save": "permission:projects.write",
        "delete": "permission:projects.delete",
    }

    def view(self, ctx):
        query = unicode(ctx.getParameter("q") or "").strip()[:120]
        page = _page(ctx)
        rows = list(ProjectModel.where(
            "owner_id = ? AND name LIKE ?", ctx.output["current_user"]["id"],
            "%" + query + "%").orderBy("id DESC").limit(21).offset((page - 1) * 20))
        base = ctx.ctxPath + "/t/tracker/project?q=" + quote(query.encode("utf-8"))
        ctx.output["projects"] = rows[:20]
        ctx.output["q"] = query
        ctx.output["page"] = page
        ctx.output["previous_url"] = base + "&page=%d" % (page - 1) if page > 1 else None
        ctx.output["next_url"] = base + "&page=%d" % (page + 1) if len(rows) > 20 else None
        ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "project")

    def edit(self, ctx):
        identity = ctx.getParameter("id")
        row = _project(ctx, identity) if identity else None
        if identity and row is None:
            return
        ctx.output["project"] = row
        ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "edit")

    def save(self, ctx):
        """POST"""
        identity = ctx.getParameter("id")
        row = _project(ctx, identity) if identity else None
        if identity and row is None:
            return
        name = unicode(ctx.getParameter("name") or "").strip()
        if not name or len(name) > 120:
            ctx.output["project"] = {"id": identity, "name": name}
            ctx.output["error"] = "Enter a project name of 1 to 120 characters."
            ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "edit")
            return
        if row is None:
            row = ProjectModel()
            row.set("owner_id", ctx.output["current_user"]["id"])
        row.set("name", name)
        row.saveIt()
        ctx.go_to = ctx.ctxPath + "/t/tracker/project"

    def delete(self, ctx):
        """POST"""
        row = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("id"))
        if row is None:
            return
        row.delete()
        ctx.go_to = ctx.ctxPath + "/t/tracker/project"

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
import re
from java.sql import Blob
from models import Task as TaskModel, Attachment, Soad_auth_user
from default.tracker.project import _id, _fail, _project, _page
from default.tracker.layout import Layout
from utils import render


def _task(ctx, project, identity):
    row = TaskModel.first("id = ? AND project_id = ?", _id(identity) or -1,
                          project.getId())
    if row is None:
        _fail(ctx, 404, "Task not found")
    return row


def _form(ctx, project, task, error=None):
    ctx.output["project"] = project
    ctx.output["task"] = task
    # Never pass entire authentication models (including password fields) to a view.
    ctx.output["people"] = [
        {"id": user.getId(), "full_name": user.get("full_name")}
        for user in Soad_auth_user.where("status = ?", "active").orderBy("full_name ASC")]
    ctx.output["error"] = error
    ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "edit")


class Task(Layout):
    ACCESS_POLICY = {
        "view": "permission:tasks.read",
        "data": "permission:tasks.read",
        "download": "permission:tasks.read",
        "edit": "permission:tasks.write",
        "save": "permission:tasks.write",
        "delete": "permission:tasks.write",
    }

    def _rows(self, ctx, project):
        status = str(ctx.getParameter("status") or "")
        if status and status not in ("todo", "doing", "done"):
            _fail(ctx, 400, "Invalid task status")
            return None
        page = _page(ctx)
        query = TaskModel.where("project_id = ?", project.getId())
        if status:
            query = TaskModel.where("project_id = ? AND status = ?", project.getId(), status)
        rows = list(query.orderBy("id DESC").limit(21).offset((page - 1) * 20))
        base = "%s/t/tracker/task?project_id=%s&status=%s" % (
            ctx.ctxPath, project.getId(), status)
        ctx.output["status"] = status
        ctx.output["page"] = page
        ctx.output["previous_url"] = base + "&page=%d" % (page - 1) if page > 1 else None
        ctx.output["next_url"] = base + "&page=%d" % (page + 1) if len(rows) > 20 else None
        return rows[:20]

    def view(self, ctx):
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        rows = self._rows(ctx, project)
        if rows is None:
            return
        ctx.output["project"] = project
        ctx.output["tasks"] = rows
        ctx.go_to = render.as_view(ctx, "task")

    def data(self, ctx):
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        rows = self._rows(ctx, project)
        if rows is None:
            return
        ctx.page_layout = False
        ctx.go_to = render.as_json(ctx, {"tasks": [
            {"id": row.getId(), "title": row.get("title"), "status": row.get("status")}
            for row in rows], "page": ctx.output["page"],
            "has_next": bool(ctx.output.get("next_url"))})

    def edit(self, ctx):
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        identity = ctx.getParameter("id")
        row = _task(ctx, project, identity) if identity else None
        if identity and row is None:
            return
        _form(ctx, project, row)

    def save(self, ctx):
        """POST"""
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        identity = ctx.getParameter("id")
        row = _task(ctx, project, identity) if identity else None
        if identity and row is None:
            return
        title = unicode(ctx.getParameter("title") or "").strip()
        status = str(ctx.getParameter("status") or "")
        assignee = str(ctx.getParameter("assignee_id") or "").strip()
        draft = {"id": identity, "title": title, "status": status, "assignee_id": assignee}
        error = None
        if not title or len(title) > 200:
            error = "Enter a task title of 1 to 200 characters."
        elif status not in ("todo", "doing", "done"):
            error = "Choose todo, doing, or done."
        elif assignee and Soad_auth_user.first("id = ? AND status = ?", assignee, "active") is None:
            error = "Choose an active application user."
        # WebContext.getParameter returns Java String; files require the wrapper.
        upload = ctx.getRequest().getParameter("attachment")
        if upload and (not hasattr(upload, "getBytes") or upload.getSize() > 1048576):
            error = "Choose a file no larger than 1 MiB."
        if error:
            _form(ctx, project, draft, error)
            return
        if row is None:
            row = TaskModel()
            row.set("project_id", project.getId())
        row.set("title", title)
        row.set("status", status)
        row.set("assignee_id", assignee or None)
        row.saveIt()
        existing = Attachment.first("task_id = ?", row.getId())
        if ctx.getParameter("remove_attachment") == "yes" and existing is not None:
            existing.delete()
            existing = None
        if upload:
            attached = existing if existing is not None else Attachment()
            attached.set("task_id", row.getId())
            # ASCII, bounded, and safe for a quoted Content-Disposition filename.
            filename = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._-]", "_", unicode(upload.getFileName()))[:120]
            attached.set("filename", filename if filename.strip(".") else "download.bin")
            attached.set("content", upload.getBytes())
            attached.saveIt()
        ctx.go_to = "%s/t/tracker/task?project_id=%s" % (ctx.ctxPath, project.getId())

    def download(self, ctx):
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        row = _task(ctx, project, ctx.getParameter("id"))
        if row is None:
            return
        attached = Attachment.first("task_id = ?", row.getId())
        if attached is None:
            _fail(ctx, 404, "No attachment")
            return
        ctx.page_layout = False
        ctx.getResponse().setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
        ctx.getResponse().setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store")
        content = attached.get("content")
        if isinstance(content, Blob):
            content = content.getBytes(1, int(content.length()))
        ctx.go_to = render.as_blob(ctx, content,
                                  "application/octet-stream", attached.get("filename"),
                                  attachment=True)

    def delete(self, ctx):
        """POST"""
        project = _project(ctx, ctx.getParameter("project_id"))
        if project is None:
            return
        row = _task(ctx, project, ctx.getParameter("id"))
        if row is None:
            return
        row.delete()
        ctx.go_to = "%s/t/tracker/task?project_id=%s" % (ctx.ctxPath, project.getId())

class Layout(object):
    ACCESS_POLICY = {"view": "authenticated", "page_layout": "authenticated"}

    def page_layout(self, ctx):
        return ("tracker", "layout", "layout")

    def view(self, ctx):
        # Shared layout data can be prepared here.
        pass
