docs.title: Install in the IDE
docs.text:
1. Use a fresh default application database. Initialize local authenticated security and the admin/member roles, then configure permissions exactly as shown in the JSON plan using the application Roles and permissions editor.
  2. Apply schema.sql after the auth schema exists, then Introspect.
  3. Create tracker/layout, tracker/project, and tracker/task in that order. Paste their source and views into the matching transaction editor files.
  4. Upload the compiled stylesheet to assets/tracker/tracker.css with File Manager.
  5. Set the Welcome transaction to tracker/project. Sign in using an application account, then open /t/tracker/project.

For CLI editing, create the transactions remotely first, then copy each controller/view into its nested src/group/code location and push it. Global assets and database SQL use their own upload/migration workflow.

docs.title: Build the CSS
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cd docs/examples/tracker
npm ci
npm run build:css

The compiled stylesheet is committed for direct use. It has no browser CDN dependency. Node/Tailwind are build tools; they are not needed by the deployed JVM.

docs.title: Prepare a container release
docs.text:
From the repository root, with Java 21 and app/lib built:

java -cp 'app/lib/*' org.python.util.jython -B \
  docs/examples/tracker/tools/prepare.py docs/examples/tracker/release

The preparation tool requires a new destination and refuses to overwrite one. It copies the example webapp, uses the real framework manifest generator to produce checksummed metadata/MySQL/H2 SQL, checks the controllers with the IDE's static policy audit, and adds the application Dockerfile. It does not access a database or deploy anything.

The script lives at docs/examples/tracker/tools/prepare.py in the repository; verification/development scripts are excluded from the published website. Use the Docker chapter for the complete build and database installation sequence.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
From the repository root:

./dev.sh build
python3 docs/examples/tracker/tests/smoke.py

The test prepares a temporary runtime, installs auth/business SQL into an isolated H2 database in MySQL mode, starts the real Jetty/Jython application on an available port, creates disposable accounts, and uses HTTP cookie sessions. It exercises CSRF, ownership, role denial, form validation, escaping, CRUD, assignment, pagination, JSON, uploads, downloads, and deletion. It terminates its server and removes its temporary runtime/database afterward.

It does not contact a live IDE or change your development database. It does not replace testing MySQL, real SMTP/TOTP delivery, browser interactions, or a Docker/Kubernetes deployment in your target environment.

docs.title: Deliberate limits
docs.text:
Assignment does not share access; only the project owner sees its records. The administrator deletion permission does not bypass ownership. Accounts are managed through built-in auth, and business rows do not hold credentials.

Each task has at most one nonempty attachment of at most 1 MiB. Uploading replaces the existing attachment; selecting remove and uploading together replaces it. Empty file selection preserves the old attachment. After validation errors, the browser requires you to choose the file again.

Writes use normal request transactions. The tutorial uses last-write-wins; add optimistic concurrency if your workflow needs conflict detection. It has no background notification worker or malware-scanning integration.

docs.title: AI assistant workflows
docs.text:
The SØAD IDE includes an AI assistant that builds and edits transactions for you from a plain-language description. You tell it what you want — "create a contact CRUD", "add an email field to the signup form", "why is the invoice page throwing an error?" — and it uses the same building blocks you do (transactions, views, the database schema) to do the work.

Ordinary transaction-editor source changes are staged for review. The IDE also supports optional auto-accept and a separate whole-app generation workflow that can execute SQL and install provisional source. Read S0ADM and AI before using these modes against valuable data.

docs.title: Enabling the assistant
docs.text:
The assistant talks to a model that you provide (bring-your-own-key), through one of three provider families:

Provider Wire protocol Use it for OpenAI compatible /chat/completions OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, and local servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LM Studio OpenAI Responses /responses OpenAI's Responses API Anthropic /messages Claude models

Whichever you pick, you configure the same four things:

Setting Description Example AI features Master switch. When disabled, the AI button, the Edit with AI link and the dashboard prompt are all hidden Enabled Endpoint The provider's base URL (the request path is appended automatically) https://api.anthropic.com/v1 API key Your provider key sk-ant-… Model The model name to use claude-sonnet-4-5

Leaving the endpoint blank is fine for the OpenAI Responses and Anthropic families — they default to https://api.openai.com/v1 and https://api.anthropic.com/v1. An OpenAI-compatible provider always needs an explicit endpoint, since the endpoint is the choice of gateway.

There are two ways to set them.

docs.title: From the IDE (self-hosted)
docs.text: Go to System Settings → Applications → <your application> → AI assistant (superadmin only), pick the provider, fill in the endpoint, API key and model, and save. This is the quickest way on a self-hosted instance. The settings are platform-wide: one provider serves every application, whichever application's page you open them from.

docs.title: From configuration / environment (managed)
docs.text:
Set them in sufia.properties or as environment variables — the usual way to inject config in a container or Kubernetes deployment.

Property Environment variable ai.enabled ai_enabled ai.provider ai_provider ai.endpoint ai_endpoint ai.api.key ai_api_key ai.model ai_model ai.auto.accept ai_auto_accept

ai.provider accepts openai, openai-responses or anthropic; any other value (a gateway brand name such as deepseek) is treated as OpenAI-compatible. ai.enabled defaults to true — set it to false to ship an instance with no AI entry points at all.

When the same value is set in more than one place, the order of precedence is, per field:

in-IDE AI assistant settings → environment variable → sufia.properties → built-in default.

Note

If the assistant reports that it is not configured, no endpoint / key / model has been resolved from any of the sources above.

docs.title: Opening the assistant
docs.text:
Open a transaction in the editor and click the AI button in the toolbar to slide out the chat panel. You can also click Edit with AI in the editor footer to open the panel pre-focused on the transaction you're viewing.

Type what you want and send (⌘/Ctrl + Enter). The assistant streams its thinking and shows each step it takes ("Reading schema for table contact", "Writing contact.py", and so on).

docs.title: The approval gate
docs.text:
In ordinary editor chat with auto-accept disabled, prepared source changes appear in a review with a before/after diff for every file:

  • Approve & Execute — write the changes to the server (and, for a new transaction, open it in the editor).
  • Discard — throw the staged work away.

Workflow differences

Auto-accept defaults off; enabling it can automate eligible approval actions. Whole-app generation can mutate the schema and provisional source before final publication. Rename/move and project-memory operations have their own behavior and are not ordinary staged source edits.

docs.title: What you can ask it to do
Create a transaction
docs.text:
Describe the transaction you want. If you don't say which group and code to use, the assistant asks first rather than guessing — so the URL and file layout are what you expect.

"Create a CRUD for the product table in group catalog."

docs.title: Build a whole app
docs.text:
Ask for several transactions at once and the assistant builds and wires them together in one go. For a multi-part request it chooses sensible group/code names itself.

"Build a booking app: a room list, a booking form, and a room CRUD."

The review shows each transaction as its own card; Approve & Execute commits them together.

docs.title: Security for generated apps
docs.text:
For a whole-app request, the assistant classifies the app as public, authenticated, or mixed, then includes explicit action policies, roles, permissions, login/logout behavior, and CSRF protection in the plan. Internal business apps default to application-local identity; landing pages and other intentionally public apps do not receive unnecessary user management.

Administrators can later keep the action policies and replace local identity with a custom application provider. See Application Security and Authentication Providers for the inference rules, provider contract, switching procedure, rollback, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Edit an existing transaction
docs.text:
Open a transaction (or use Edit with AI) and describe the change. The assistant reads the current files first and stages a focused edit.

"Add an email column to the form and validate it."

docs.title: Rename or move a transaction
docs.text:
Ask it to change a transaction's group and/or code. Because a rename also updates the controller class name and the default view, the assistant states the exact rename and asks you to confirm in chat first — and then applies it immediately.

"Rename orders/cart to shop/basket."

Note

A rename doesn't rewrite your own internal references (links, explicit view names). The assistant will remind you to check those.

docs.title: Roll back to a previous version
docs.text:
Every save is versioned. If a change didn't work out, ask the assistant to restore an earlier version. It lists the saved versions, you pick one, and it stages that version as a change so you review the diff before approving. Approving snapshots the current state first, so a restore is itself reversible.

"Show me the versions of catalog/product and restore yesterday's."

docs.title: Diagnose data problems
docs.text:
When something looks wrong (a missing record, an unexpected value), the assistant can run read-only queries to inspect the actual rows before suggesting a fix.

"The dashboard total is wrong — can you check the orders data?"

docs.title: Debug runtime errors
docs.text:
If a page is throwing or misbehaving, reproduce it, then ask the assistant. It reads the server log to find the real error and stack trace, then proposes a fix based on what actually happened instead of guessing.

"The invoice page returns a 500 — what's wrong?"

docs.title: Schema changes and SQL
docs.text:
In ordinary editor chat the assistant can read schema and suggest SQL for the developer's Execute button. Authorized whole-app generation additionally has a direct SQL execution path. For a normal editor SQL block:

  • Review the SQL.
  • Click Execute to run it against your application database.
  • After a structural change the models are refreshed automatically, so new columns and tables are immediately available.

Warning

For this editor workflow, read SQL before clicking Execute — destructive statements (for example DROP) are blocked, but you are still the one applying the change.

docs.title: Project memory (AGENTS.md)
docs.text:
The assistant already knows the SØAD framework, but it doesn't know your project's conventions. You can teach it by keeping notes in a file at WEB-INF/AGENTS.md. Anything in that file — design decisions, naming conventions, UI guidelines, domain rules — is treated as authoritative guidance on every request.

Two ways to maintain it:

  • Edit it yourself in the File Manager (it's a normal Markdown file).
  • Ask the assistant to remember something — say "remember this" or "save to memory" and it appends the note for you.

"Remember: all money amounts are stored in cents, and we always soft-delete."

AGENTS.md is optional. When it's empty, the assistant just uses its built-in framework knowledge.

docs.title: Designing larger apps with a planner
docs.text:
The assistant is a builder — it's at its best turning a clear, focused request into transactions you approve. For a larger app — many screens, a real data model, cross-cutting conventions — it pays to design first, then build.

A workflow that works well:

  1. Plan with a capable "frontier" AI. Use a strong general-purpose model (the kind you'd reach for to architect and design) to turn your idea into a concrete plan: the data model, the list of transactions, how they link, and your conventions.
  2. Give the planner SØAD's context. So its plan uses SØAD conventions rather than generic ones, provide it with SØAD's coding context (the framework documentation) and the planning guide below — the guide tells it how to shape a plan the assistant can build cleanly.
  3. Split the result into two streams:
    • Durable conventions (naming, money handling, soft-delete, UI standards) go into your project's AGENTS.md once — they then apply to every request.
    • The build plan (data model + transactions) goes into the chat, fed phase by phase.
  4. Build in order: run the schema SQL first (Execute), then paste the transactions a batch at a time, approving each before moving on.

This split isn't arbitrary: AGENTS.md is always in the assistant's context, while chat history is finite and trims older turns. Put "always true" in AGENTS.md and "what to build now" in chat.

Planning guide

Give this to your planning AI, alongside SØAD's coding context, so it produces plans shaped for the assistant to build:

Read the SØAD Planning Guide

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text: The panel keeps your chat history per transaction, so you can close it and come back later. Use New chat to start a fresh conversation (clearing the context), and All conversations to browse past chats.

docs.title: Safety and scope
docs.text:
The assistant is deliberately constrained:

  • Ordinary editor file changes use staged review; optional auto-accept changes the interaction. Rename/move and project-memory updates are separate operations.
  • Ordinary editor SQL is developer-executed. Server-authorized empty-app generation can execute SQL and install provisional transactions.
  • Transaction version restoration stages source changes. It is not a database restore or production release rollback. Use the release/deployment tools for those separate operational workflows.

What is sent to the model

To do its work, the assistant sends relevant context to your configured model provider — your request, the transaction files it's working on, schema details, and, when debugging, log excerpts. Choose a provider you trust with your project data, and be aware that anything present in the server log (which the log tool may read) can be included when you ask it to debug.

docs.title: Tips for good results
docs.text:
• Be specific about names. Give the group and code when you have a preference; otherwise the assistant will ask.
  • Mention the tables and columns involved — the assistant reads the schema, but naming them removes ambiguity.
  • Work in small steps and approve as you go; it's easier to review a focused diff than a sweeping one.
  • Reproduce an error first, then ask — the assistant reads the log, so a fresh error trail helps it find the cause.
  • Capture conventions in AGENTS.md once, instead of repeating them in every chat.
  • Plan big apps first. For anything large, design it with a planner and feed it in phases — see Designing larger apps with a planner.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause / fix "AI assistant is not configured" No endpoint / key / model resolved — set them in System Settings → Applications → AI assistant or via the ai.* properties/environment variables. No AI button, no dashboard prompt The feature is switched off — set AI features to Enabled, or ai.enabled = true / ai_enabled=true. Requests fail with an auth error Wrong API key, or the model name isn't valid for your provider. Nothing happens / provider error Check the endpoint base URL, and that the selected provider matches the API the endpoint actually speaks (/chat/completions, /responses or /messages). Claude replies are cut off mid-file Raise ai.max.output.tokens (Anthropic defaults to 8192 output tokens). A change didn't take effect Confirm you clicked Approve & Execute — staged changes aren't written until you do. The model doesn't see a new column/table Run the suggested SQL with Execute (which refreshes the models), or Introspect the datasource.

docs.title: Planning applications with AI
docs.text:
Read this together with the developer chapters. They teach the SØAD framework (Jython transactions, Handlebars views, ActiveJDBC models, routing, hard rules). This file tells you how to turn a request into a build plan that a second AI — the SØAD IDE agent — will implement.

You are the architect. You do not write the final code here; you produce a clear, staged plan. The agent is the builder: it reads your plan, generates the transactions. Specify the intended review points and generation mode in the plan.

docs.title: How the builder works (plan within these constraints)
docs.text:
• Decompose the app into transaction-sized units, each doing one job. Ordinary editor source changes are staged; whole-app generation can coordinate multiple transactions and install provisional source during validation.
  • Put schema SQL before dependent controllers. Editor-chat SQL uses the developer Execute action; server-authorized whole-app generation can execute DDL/DML. State which workflow and database the plan targets.
  • It asks for group/code if you don't specify them (for a single transaction). So always name the group and code for every transaction.
  • It already knows SØAD idioms — routing, the POST/PRG pattern, model naming, default-view resolution, the built-in helpers. Specify intent, not mechanics. Don't re-teach the framework or hand-write boilerplate the agent will produce correctly on its own.
  • Phase the plan into reviewable chunks. Account for the selected auto-accept setting and whole-app workflow rather than promising a click before every write.
  • Its context is bounded. Keep the plan tight and concrete; for a big app, split it so it can be fed and approved in stages rather than one huge block.
  • Separate development from release operations. A source restoration is not a database rollback; deployment needs its own migration and verification plan.

docs.title: What to produce
docs.text:
Output a plan with these parts, in this order:

  1. Data model — the tables, columns and relationships, with the CREATE TABLE SQL when the tables don't already exist. This runs first (human clicks Execute).
  2. Transactions — one block per transaction (see the template). This is the bulk of the plan and maps 1:1 onto what the builder creates.
  3. Phases — group the transactions into approval-sized batches, in build order (schema → core entities → screens that depend on them → wiring).
  4. Project conventions (optional) — durable rules the builder should always follow (naming, money handling, soft-delete, UI conventions). These belong in the project's AGENTS.md, not repeated in every request — call them out separately.

docs.title: Style rules (what makes a plan land well)
docs.text:
• Name group/code explicitly for every transaction — it becomes the URL /t/<group>/<code> and the file layout. Never leave it to the builder to guess.
  • Name tables and columns. The builder reads the schema, but naming them removes ambiguity and prevents wrong assumptions.
  • Schema first. If tables don't exist, give the DDL up front so the build targets real columns.
  • One responsibility per transaction. Prefer catalog/room (CRUD) + booking/new (a form) over one mega-transaction.
  • Specify behaviour, not framework code. Say "list with a link to the form, soft-delete on the row" — not how to wire render.as_view or the PRG redirect.
  • Describe the actions each transaction needs (e.g. view, list, save, delete) and any per-action method (a save is a POST).
  • State the fields and validation (required, type, unique) — these drive both the form and the controller.
  • Wire the screens together. Say which list links to which form/detail, so the built transactions form one app rather than isolated pages.
  • Phase to approval batches. "These 3 transactions" is one reviewable diff; a 20-transaction dump is not.
  • Flag anything that needs SQL (schema change, seed data) as a fenced sql block for a human to Execute — never assume the builder ran it.

  ...
### Schema SQL (run first, via Execute)

catalog/room
